Information regarding precipitation was obtained from publications by Landers (1970), the U.S. Environmental Science Services Administration (1968), Miller, et al. (1963), and Hardy (1970).
The project area is located in a water surplus area. The windward slopes of the mountains have a heavy annual precipitation of 70 to 80 inches per year, placing the site in one of the highest precipitation regions of the eastern United States. Mean annual precipitation for the mountain climatological division of South Carolina is 69 to 71 inches per year. There are about 50 to 70 days of thunderstorms per year in this area. The least amount of monthly precipitation for the period 1941 to 1970 occurred in September 1954, when only 0.65 inch of rain was recorded. The maximum for this period occurred in July 1941, when 16.91 inches were recorded. Normally the heaviest rainfall comes during the month of March and during the late summer while the driest period is in the fall. Snowfall is limited over most of North and South Carolina, but accumulations of 6 to 9 inches occur in the mountainous areas. Maximum snowfall records were set in South Carolina in 1969, with the zone of the greatest fall in the Lower Piedmont and Sandhills regions to the south and east of the Bad Creek site. Maximum snowfall has been recorded at Nashville and Mount Mitchell in North Carolina.
The mean annual class A pan evaporation rate is about 50 inches per year, while mean lake evaporation is approximately 39 inches per year, and average runoff is about 30 inches per year. These figures are consistent with the mean annual precipitation figure shown above for the mountain climatological division.
Severe droughts occur in South Carolina on an average of once every 15 years, with less severe droughts on a less widespread basis occurring once every 7 to 8 years (Landers, 1970). Due to the high annual precipitation, the Bad Creek area is probably much less affected by droughts than other areas in South Carolina.
